scenes.heading: Compaction
scenes.narration: Compaction merges many small files into fewer large ones, curing the performance drag of fragmented storage.

scenes.heading: Why small files hurt
bullets: Each file adds open and metadata overhead.
Query planners struggle with huge file counts.
Streaming and frequent writes create fragments.
Compaction rewrites them into optimal sizes.
scenes.narration: Every file a query touches costs time to open and track, so thousands of tiny files slow everything down. Streaming ingestion and frequent small writes are the usual culprits behind this fragmentation. Compaction rewrites those fragments into fewer, larger files sized for efficient reads.

scenes.heading: How compaction runs
steps: Swap in and clean up old files
scenes.narration: A compaction job first identifies partitions choked with small files. It reads those files, combines their rows, and writes fresh files at a target size. It then atomically swaps the new files in and removes the old ones once no query still needs them.

scenes.heading: Triggering compaction on a table
scenes.narration: The OPTIMIZE command bin-packs small files in the chosen partition into larger ones for faster scans. VACUUM then physically deletes files that compaction made obsolete, once a safe retention window has passed. Together they reclaim performance and storage without disturbing live queries.

scenes.text: Compaction consolidates many small files into fewer large ones, restoring query speed lost to fragmentation from streaming and frequent writes.
scenes.narration: Schedule compaction regularly on high-write tables, and you keep the small-file problem from quietly eroding performance.
